medicines.name: Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate
medicines.description: Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate is an oral prodrug of tenofovir, an acyclic nucleotide (adenosine monophosphate) analogue. After intracellular phosphorylation to tenofovir diphosphate it competes with natural nucleotides and terminates DNA chain elongation, inhibiting HIV-1 reverse transcriptase and the hepatitis B virus polymerase. It is used with other antiretrovirals for HIV-1 treatment, as HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis with emtricitabine, and as a first-line agent for chronic hepatitis B because of its high barrier to resistance.
medicines.dosage_text: Adults and pediatric patients weighing at least 35 kg (HIV-1 infection, in combination with other antiretrovirals; chronic hepatitis B): 300 mg orally once daily, with or without food. Renal impairment (adults): CrCl 30-49 mL/min, 300 mg every 48 hours; CrCl 10-29 mL/min, 300 mg every 72-96 hours; hemodialysis, 300 mg every 7 days or after a total of about 12 hours of dialysis; no dosing recommendation is available for CrCl < 10 mL/min without hemodialysis. Serum creatinine, estimated creatinine clearance, urine glucose and urine protein are assessed before and during therapy, with serum phosphorus in chronic kidney disease. Refer to current product labeling.
medicines.storage: Store at room temperature as directed on the product labeling.
medicines.black_box_warning: Severe acute exacerbation of hepatitis B: severe acute exacerbations of hepatitis B have been reported in HBV-infected patients who have discontinued anti-hepatitis B therapy, including tenofovir disoproxil fumarate. Hepatic function is monitored closely with clinical and laboratory follow-up for at least several months after discontinuation; resumption of anti-hepatitis B therapy may be warranted.
medicines.source_attribution: VIREAD (tenofovir disoproxil fumarate) FDA label via DailyMed; StatPearls: Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors; StatPearls: HIV and AIDS; StatPearls: Hepatitis B; Goodman & Gilman's 14th ed.
indications: HIV-1 infection in adults and pediatric patients 2 years and older weighing at least 10 kg, in combination with other antiretroviral agents
Chronic hepatitis B in adults and pediatric patients 2 years and older weighing at least 10 kg
HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), in combination with emtricitabine
HIV post-exposure prophylaxis as part of a combination regimen (e.g., with emtricitabine plus dolutegravir)
Reduction of mother-to-child transmission of hepatitis B in HBsAg- and/or HBeAg-positive pregnant women
adverse: Nausea, diarrhea, headache, asthenia, rash and depression (most common in HIV trials)
New-onset or worsening renal impairment, including acute renal failure and Fanconi syndrome (proximal tubulopathy)
Decreased bone mineral density and mineralization defects (osteomalacia associated with proximal tubulopathy)
Severe acute exacerbation of hepatitis B after discontinuation
Lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis (reported with nucleoside analogues)
Immune reconstitution syndrome in HIV, including autoimmune disorders (e.g., Graves' disease)
contraindications: No contraindications are listed in the US label
Not used alone for HIV-1 treatment; used only in combination with other antiretroviral agents
HIV-1 antibody testing is required before starting for hepatitis B, because use as the only active agent in untreated HIV may select resistant HIV-1
Avoided with concurrent or recent use of nephrotoxic agents (e.g., high-dose or multiple NSAIDs)
No dosing recommendation for CrCl < 10 mL/min in patients not on hemodialysis
interactions: Nephrotoxic drugs and drugs eliminated by active tubular secretion (e.g., acyclovir, valacyclovir, ganciclovir, valganciclovir, cidofovir, aminoglycosides such as gentamicin): may raise tenofovir or co-drug concentrations and add renal toxicity.
NSAIDs (high-dose or multiple): acute renal failure has been reported after starting them in HIV-infected patients with renal risk factors; the combination is avoided.
Ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitors (atazanavir/ritonavir, lopinavir/ritonavir, darunavir/ritonavir): increase tenofovir concentrations; monitor for tenofovir-associated adverse reactions.
Ledipasvir/sofosbuvir, sofosbuvir/velpatasvir and sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir: increase tenofovir exposure; monitor for tenofovir-associated adverse reactions, especially renal.
Didanosine: tenofovir increases didanosine concentrations; the combination requires dose modification and close monitoring.

medicines.name: Entecavir
medicines.description: Entecavir is a guanosine nucleoside analogue that is phosphorylated intracellularly to its active triphosphate, which competes with deoxyguanosine triphosphate and inhibits all three activities of the hepatitis B virus polymerase (base priming, reverse transcription of the negative strand and synthesis of the positive strand). It is a preferred first-line oral agent for chronic hepatitis B because of its potency and high barrier to resistance in nucleoside-naive patients.
medicines.dosage_text: Adults (chronic hepatitis B): nucleoside-inhibitor-treatment-naive with compensated liver disease, 0.5 mg orally once daily; lamivudine-refractory or known lamivudine/telbivudine resistance, 1 mg once daily; decompensated liver disease, 1 mg once daily. Take on an empty stomach (at least 2 hours after a meal and 2 hours before the next meal). Renal impairment (usual 0.5 mg dose): CrCl 30 to < 50 mL/min, 0.25 mg once daily or 0.5 mg every 48 hours; CrCl 10 to < 30, 0.15 mg once daily or 0.5 mg every 72 hours; CrCl < 10, hemodialysis or CAPD, 0.05 mg once daily or 0.5 mg every 7 days (give after hemodialysis); the 1 mg regimens are adjusted proportionally. No dose adjustment for hepatic impairment. Refer to current product labeling.
medicines.storage: Store tablets at 20-25 C (68-77 F), excursions permitted to 15-30 C, in a tightly closed container protected from light.
medicines.black_box_warning: Severe acute exacerbations of hepatitis B have been reported in patients who discontinued anti-hepatitis B therapy, including entecavir; hepatic function is monitored closely for at least several months after discontinuation. Patients coinfected with HIV and HBV: entecavir is not recommended for HBV in coinfected patients not also receiving highly active antiretroviral therapy because of the risk of HIV-1 resistance. Lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis, including fatal cases, have been reported with nucleoside analogues.
medicines.source_attribution: BARACLUDE (entecavir) FDA label via DailyMed; StatPearls: Hepatitis B; Goodman & Gilman's 14th ed.
indications: Chronic hepatitis B in adults with evidence of active viral replication and either persistent aminotransferase elevation or histologically active disease
Chronic hepatitis B in pediatric patients 2 years and older (weight-based dosing)
Lamivudine-refractory chronic hepatitis B (higher 1 mg dose)
Chronic hepatitis B with decompensated liver disease (1 mg dose)
Acute hepatitis B when antiviral treatment is warranted (preferred with tenofovir because of a high resistance barrier)
adverse: Headache, fatigue, dizziness and nausea (most common, >= 3%)
Severe acute exacerbation of hepatitis B after discontinuation
Lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis (nucleoside analogue class effect)
Selection of HIV-1 resistance when used in HIV/HBV coinfection without antiretroviral therapy
contraindications: No contraindications are listed in the US label
HIV/HBV coinfection in patients not receiving fully suppressive antiretroviral therapy (risk of HIV-1 resistance)
Treatment is suspended in any patient who develops clinical or laboratory findings suggestive of lactic acidosis or pronounced hepatotoxicity
Dose adjustment is required when CrCl < 50 mL/min
interactions: Drugs that reduce renal function: may increase serum concentrations of entecavir or of the co-administered drug (entecavir is mainly renally eliminated).
Drugs that compete for active tubular secretion: may increase serum concentrations of entecavir or of the co-administered drug; monitor for adverse reactions.
Cyclosporine or tacrolimus in liver transplant recipients: renal function must be carefully monitored before and during entecavir therapy.
Food: the label directs administration on an empty stomach (at least 2 hours after and 2 hours before a meal).

medicines.name: Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir (TLD)
medicines.generic_name: Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 300 mg + lamivudine 300 mg + dolutegravir 50 mg
medicines.description: TLD is a once-daily fixed-dose tablet combining two nucleos(t)ide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (tenofovir disoproxil fumarate and lamivudine), which terminate viral DNA chain synthesis, with dolutegravir, an integrase strand transfer inhibitor that blocks integration of HIV DNA into the host genome. WHO recommends dolutegravir-based therapy as the preferred first- and second-line HIV treatment in all populations, and tenofovir plus lamivudine also suppress hepatitis B virus. There is no US boxed warning for this WHO-prequalified combination itself, but the US label of its tenofovir disoproxil component carries a boxed warning for severe acute exacerbation of hepatitis B after discontinuation, which applies to people with HBV co-infection. In the Philippines it is the DOH's recommended first-line antiretroviral regimen, procured nationally for people living with HIV (Philippine News Agency, July 2026).
medicines.dosage_text: Adults and adolescents weighing at least 30 kg: one tablet (dolutegravir 50 mg / lamivudine 300 mg / tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 300 mg) orally once daily, with or without food. With rifampicin, the dolutegravir dose is increased to 50 mg twice daily (an additional dolutegravir 50 mg tablet about 12 hours after TLD). Not recommended when CrCl < 50 mL/min (use separate components with dose adjustment). No dose adjustment for mild or moderate hepatic impairment; caution in severe hepatic impairment. Refer to current product labeling.
medicines.storage: Store as directed on the product labeling.
medicines.source_attribution: WHO Public Assessment Report (WHOPAR) product information for dolutegravir/lamivudine/tenofovir disoproxil 50/300/300 mg; WHO news release 22 July 2019 (dolutegravir preferred in all populations); TIVICAY (dolutegravir) FDA label via DailyMed; NIH Adult and Adolescent ARV Guidelines drug-interaction tables; StatPearls: HIV and AIDS; Goodman & Gilman's 14th ed; DOH via Philippine News Agency (2026)
indications: HIV-1 infection in adults and adolescents weighing at least 30 kg (WHO-preferred first-line regimen)
Treatment-experienced adults and adolescents, as a dolutegravir-based regimen (WHO-preferred second-line option)
HIV treatment in pregnant women and women of childbearing potential (WHO recommends dolutegravir as preferred in all populations)
HIV/hepatitis B coinfection, where a tenofovir-containing regimen is preferred because tenofovir and lamivudine are active against HBV
adverse: Diarrhea, nausea and headache (most frequent)
Hypersensitivity reactions with rash and severe liver effects (dolutegravir); stop immediately if severe
Weight gain (integrase inhibitor class, greater than with protease inhibitors or NNRTIs)
Renal toxicity from tenofovir disoproxil: proximal tubulopathy (Fanconi syndrome), acute or chronic renal insufficiency
Decreased bone mineral density (tenofovir disoproxil)
Severe acute exacerbation of hepatitis B after discontinuation in coinfected patients
Lactic acidosis (rare) and immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to dolutegravir, lamivudine, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or excipients
Co-administration with dofetilide (OCT2 substrate with a narrow therapeutic window)
Co-administration with fampridine (dalfampridine)
Creatinine clearance < 50 mL/min (fixed-dose combination not recommended)
Body weight below 30 kg (fixed-dose tablet not indicated)
interactions: Rifampicin: reduces dolutegravir exposure (about 54%); dolutegravir is given as 50 mg twice daily during co-administration.
Metformin: dolutegravir increases metformin exposure; metformin dose adjustment is considered when starting or stopping dolutegravir, with glycemic and adverse-effect monitoring.

Polyvalent cations (magnesium/aluminium antacids, laxatives, sucralfate, calcium or iron supplements, multivitamins): chelate dolutegravir and reduce its absorption; dolutegravir is given 2 hours before or 6 hours after them (calcium or iron may be taken together with dolutegravir with food).
Dofetilide and fampridine: contraindicated (dolutegravir inhibits OCT2 and raises their levels, risk of life-threatening toxicity).
Carbamazepine, phenytoin and St John's wort: reduce dolutegravir levels; co-administration is avoided per the dolutegravir label.
Ledipasvir/sofosbuvir: increases tenofovir exposure; monitor renal function.
Nephrotoxic drugs, including high-dose or multiple NSAIDs: additive renal risk with tenofovir disoproxil.

medicines.name: Co-trimoxazole (Sulfamethoxazole + Trimethoprim)
medicines.description: Co-trimoxazole combines sulfamethoxazole, which inhibits dihydropteroate synthase and blocks bacterial use of para-aminobenzoic acid, with trimethoprim, which inhibits dihydrofolate reductase. Sequential blockade of folate synthesis gives a synergistic, often bactericidal effect. It is used for urinary tract infections, shigellosis, traveler's diarrhea, exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, and for treatment and prophylaxis of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and toxoplasmosis.
medicines.dosage_text: Adults (sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim): urinary tract infection, 800/160 mg (one double-strength tablet or two single-strength tablets) every 12 hours for 10-14 days; shigellosis, 800/160 mg every 12 hours for 5 days; traveler's diarrhea, 800/160 mg every 12 hours for 5 days; acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis, 800/160 mg every 12 hours for 10-14 days; Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia treatment, 75-100 mg/kg/day sulfamethoxazole plus 15-20 mg/kg/day trimethoprim in divided doses every 6 hours for 14-21 days; P. jirovecii prophylaxis, one double-strength tablet daily. Renal impairment: CrCl > 30 mL/min usual regimen; 15-30 mL/min half the usual regimen; < 15 mL/min not recommended. Maintain adequate fluid intake to prevent crystalluria. Refer to current product labeling.
medicines.storage: Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F) in a tight, light-resistant container.
medicines.source_attribution: BACTRIM / BACTRIM DS FDA label via DailyMed; StatPearls: Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole; Goodman & Gilman's 14th ed.
indications: Urinary tract infections due to susceptible organisms
Shigellosis (enteritis due to susceptible Shigella)

Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis

Toxoplasmosis: treatment and prophylaxis

Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis), sometimes fatal
Hyperkalemia (trimethoprim, especially at high dose, in renal insufficiency or with potassium-raising drugs)
Hematologic toxicity: agranulocytosis, thrombocytopenia, anemias and myelosuppression; hemolysis in G6PD deficiency
Fulminant hepatic necrosis (rare, can be fatal)
Hypoglycemia (rare, including in non-diabetic patients; more likely with renal dysfunction or high doses)
Crystalluria, interstitial nephritis and acute kidney injury
Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea; higher adverse-reaction rates in patients with AIDS
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to trimethoprim or sulfonamides
History of drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia with trimethoprim and/or sulfonamides
Megaloblastic anemia due to folate deficiency
Infants younger than 2 months
Marked hepatic damage
Severe renal insufficiency when renal function cannot be monitored
Concomitant dofetilide
interactions: Methotrexate: additive antifolate effect increases methotrexate toxicity; the label advises avoiding concurrent use.
Warfarin: potentiated anticoagulant effect; monitor prothrombin time/INR.
ACE inhibitors, ARBs and spironolactone: additive hyperkalemia risk; the label advises avoiding concurrent ACE inhibitor use, and potassium is monitored.
Sulfonylureas: potentiated hypoglycemic effect; monitor blood glucose.
Phenytoin: prolonged phenytoin half-life; monitor phenytoin levels.
Digoxin: increased digoxin levels; monitor digoxin concentrations.
Dofetilide: concomitant use is contraindicated.
Cyclosporine: the label advises avoiding concurrent use.

medicines.name: Praziquantel
medicines.description: Praziquantel is a synthetic pyrazinoisoquinoline anthelmintic that increases the permeability of the helminth tegument to calcium, producing rapid muscle contraction, spastic paralysis and tegumental damage that exposes the parasite to host defenses. It is the drug of choice for all Schistosoma species, including S. japonicum endemic in the Philippines, and for the liver flukes Clonorchis and Opisthorchis, and is also active against tapeworms and cysticercosis.
medicines.dosage_text: Adults and children 1 year and older: schistosomiasis, 20 mg/kg three times in one day, doses 4-6 hours apart (60 mg/kg/day; StatPearls cites 40 mg/kg/day for S. mansoni, S. haematobium and S. intercalatum and 60 mg/kg/day for S. japonicum and S. mekongi); clonorchiasis/opisthorchiasis, 25 mg/kg three times in one day, 4-6 hours apart. Taeniasis (off-label): 5-10 mg/kg as a single dose. Strong CYP3A inducers such as rifampicin are stopped 2-4 weeks before praziquantel and may be restarted 1 day after completing treatment. No renal dose adjustment. Driving or operating machinery is avoided on the day of treatment and the following day. Refer to current product labeling.
medicines.source_attribution: BILTRICIDE (praziquantel) FDA label via DailyMed; StatPearls: Antiparasitic Drugs; Philippine News Agency report on the DOH schistosomiasis program; Goodman & Gilman's 14th ed.
indications: Schistosomiasis due to all Schistosoma species, including S. japonicum (endemic in parts of the Philippines)
Clonorchiasis and opisthorchiasis (liver flukes)
Mass drug administration in schistosomiasis-endemic areas under the DOH Schistosomiasis Control Program (free of charge)
Tapeworm infections (Taenia saginata, T. solium, Diphyllobothrium latum, Hymenolepis nana) (off-label)
Neurocysticercosis, with corticosteroid cover (off-label)
Paragonimiasis (Paragonimus westermani) (off-label)
adverse: Malaise, headache, dizziness and drowsiness
Abdominal discomfort with or without nausea
Fever and urticaria
Arthralgia, myalgia and skin rash
CNS reactions in neurocysticercosis from parasite destruction (seizures, raised intracranial pressure, meningismus)

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to praziquantel

medicines.name: Aciclovir
medicines.drug_class: Antiviral (nucleoside analogue, herpesvirus DNA polymerase inhibitor)
medicines.description: Aciclovir is a synthetic purine (guanosine) nucleoside analogue that is phosphorylated by viral and host cellular enzymes to aciclovir triphosphate, which inhibits herpesvirus DNA polymerase and terminates viral DNA chain elongation. Its selectivity for infected cells makes it active against herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 and varicella-zoster virus. It is used for genital and mucocutaneous herpes, herpes zoster, varicella and, intravenously, herpes simplex encephalitis.
medicines.dosage_text: Adults (oral): initial genital herpes, 200 mg every 4 hours five times daily for 10 days; chronic suppression of recurrent genital herpes, 400 mg twice daily for up to 12 months; herpes zoster, 800 mg every 4 hours five times daily for 7-10 days; varicella, 800 mg four times daily for 5 days. HSV encephalitis (IV): 10 mg/kg every 8 hours for 21 days, dosed on ideal body weight. Renal impairment (oral): 800 mg regimen, CrCl 10-25 mL/min/1.73 m2 every 8 hours and 0-10 every 12 hours; 200 mg regimen, CrCl 0-10 every 12 hours; 400 mg twice-daily regimen, CrCl 0-10, 200 mg every 12 hours. Adequate hydration is maintained. Refer to current product labeling.
medicines.storage: Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); excursions permitted to 15-30 C. Protect from moisture.
medicines.source_attribution: Acyclovir tablets FDA label (Apotex) via DailyMed; StatPearls: Acyclovir; VIREAD FDA label (drugs affecting renal function); Goodman & Gilman's 14th ed.

medicines.name: Rabies Vaccine (PVRV / PCECV)
medicines.generic_name: Rabies vaccine, inactivated: purified Vero cell (PVRV) or purified chick embryo cell (PCECV)
medicines.description: Cell-culture rabies vaccines contain inactivated rabies virus grown in Vero cells (PVRV) or chick embryo cells (PCECV). They induce virus-neutralizing antibodies, which take time to develop, so post-exposure prophylaxis combines immediate wound washing, a vaccine course and, for category III exposures, rabies immunoglobulin to cover the gap. Because clinical rabies is almost always fatal, post-exposure prophylaxis has no contraindication.
medicines.dosage_text: Post-exposure prophylaxis (category II: vaccine; category III: vaccine plus rabies immunoglobulin), previously unvaccinated persons. WHO regimens: intradermal 1-week, 2-site regimen, 0.1 mL at 2 sites on days 0, 3 and 7; intramuscular 2-week (Essen) regimen, 1 dose on days 0, 3, 7 and between day 14 and 28; intramuscular 3-week (Zagreb) regimen, 2 doses on day 0 and 1 dose on days 7 and 21. US labeling (PCECV, 1 mL IM in the deltoid, never gluteal): days 0, 3, 7, 14 and 28 with HRIG; CDC uses 4 doses (days 0, 3, 7, 14) in immunocompetent persons and a fifth dose on day 28 in immunocompromised persons. Previously vaccinated persons: WHO 1-site ID on days 0 and 3 or 4-site ID on day 0; US label 1 mL IM on days 0 and 3; no immunoglobulin. Once started, PEP is not interrupted for local or mild systemic reactions. In the Philippines, PEP is delivered through DOH-certified Animal Bite Treatment Centers and covered by the PhilHealth Animal Bite Package. Refer to current product labeling.
medicines.storage: Store at 2-8 C (36-46 F), protected from light; do not freeze; use immediately after reconstitution.
medicines.source_attribution: WHO position paper on rabies vaccines and immunoglobulins (2018) and WHO PEP recommendations page; WHO rabies fact sheet; RABAVERT (PCECV) FDA label via DailyMed; StatPearls: Rabies; PhilHealth Circular No. 015 s. 2012 (Animal Bite Package); Goodman & Gilman's 14th ed.

Post-exposure prophylaxis after category III exposure (transdermal bites or scratches, mucous membrane or broken-skin contamination with saliva), together with rabies immunoglobulin

adverse: Injection-site erythema, induration and pain
Flu-like symptoms: fatigue, fever, headache, myalgia, malaise
Arthralgia, dizziness, lymphadenopathy, nausea and rash
Hypersensitivity reactions including anaphylaxis (rare)
Neurologic events temporally associated with vaccination (rare): Guillain-Barre syndrome, encephalitis, transient paralysis, myelitis, retrobulbar neuritis
contraindications: Post-exposure prophylaxis: no contraindication, including pregnancy, because rabies is nearly always fatal
Pre-exposure vaccination: history of anaphylaxis to the vaccine or any component

interactions: Corticosteroids, other immunosuppressive agents, antimalarials and radiation therapy: may impair the antibody response; serum neutralizing antibody is checked (e.g., on day 14) when PEP is given during such therapy.
Chloroquine or hydroxychloroquine: pre-exposure vaccination is completed before starting these drugs whenever possible.
Rabies immunoglobulin: never mixed in the same syringe or injected at the same anatomical site as the vaccine.
Rabies immunoglobulin above the recommended dose, or repeated doses: can suppress active antibody production to the vaccine.

medicines.name: Rabies Immunoglobulin (HRIG / ERIG)
medicines.generic_name: Rabies immunoglobulin: human (HRIG) or purified equine (ERIG)
medicines.description: Rabies immunoglobulin provides ready-made rabies virus-neutralizing antibodies, prepared from the plasma of immunized human donors (HRIG) or from hyperimmunized horses as purified equine immunoglobulin or F(ab')2 fragments (ERIG). Infiltrated into and around the wound, it neutralizes virus at the inoculation site before vaccine-induced antibodies appear. It is used with rabies vaccine for category III exposures in persons not previously vaccinated.
medicines.dosage_text: Single dose at the start of post-exposure prophylaxis, preferably with the first vaccine dose and not beyond day 7 after the first vaccine dose. HRIG: 20 IU/kg body weight (all ages). ERIG: 40 IU/kg body weight. As much of the dose as anatomically feasible is infiltrated into and around the wound(s); WHO advises wound infiltration rather than injecting the remainder at a distant site, while US HRIG labeling gives any remainder intramuscularly at a site distant from vaccine administration. Never given in the same syringe or at the same site as vaccine, and not repeated. WHO considers skin testing before modern ERIG unnecessary. Not given to persons who were previously vaccinated. Refer to current product labeling.
medicines.storage: Store at 2-8 C (36-46 F); do not freeze. HyperRAB may be kept at room temperature up to 25 C for up to 6 months within its expiry.
medicines.source_attribution: WHO position paper on rabies vaccines and immunoglobulins (2018); HYPERRAB (rabies immune globulin, human) FDA label via DailyMed; RABAVERT FDA label; StatPearls: Rabies; Goodman & Gilman's 14th ed.

Post-exposure prophylaxis in immunocompromised persons, who receive both vaccine and immunoglobulin even after prior vaccination

medicines.name: Cetirizine
medicines.description: Cetirizine, derived from hydroxyzine, is a fast-acting, highly selective peripheral histamine H1-receptor antagonist. It crosses the blood-brain barrier only minimally, so it causes less sedation than first-generation antihistamines, and it also reduces neutrophil and eosinophil infiltration. It is used for seasonal and perennial allergic rhinitis and chronic urticaria.
medicines.dosage_text: Adults and children 12 years and older: 5-10 mg orally once daily depending on symptom severity; OTC labeling directs one 10 mg tablet once daily, not more than one in 24 hours, for ages 6-64, with adults 65 years and older asking a doctor. Renal impairment (CrCl 11-31 mL/min) or hepatic impairment: 5 mg once daily. May be taken with or without food. Refer to current product labeling.

medicines.name: Zinc Sulfate
medicines.description: Zinc is an essential trace element that serves as a cofactor for many enzymes and transcription factors involved in immunity, epithelial repair and growth. In acute diarrhea it inhibits several intracellular pathways of intestinal ion secretion (cAMP, calcium and nitric oxide) and supports mucosal recovery; WHO and UNICEF have recommended zinc with oral rehydration salts for all childhood diarrhea episodes since 2004. It is also used to correct zinc deficiency and, as zinc salts, in Wilson disease.
medicines.dosage_text: Acute or persistent diarrhea in children up to 5 years (WHO-prequalified zinc sulfate product): under 6 months, 10 mg elemental zinc once daily; 6 months to 5 years, 20 mg elemental zinc once daily; for 10-14 days together with reduced-osmolarity ORS, continued even after diarrhea stops. Adults: recommended dietary allowance 11 mg/day (men) and 8 mg/day (women), 11 mg/day in pregnancy and 12 mg/day in lactation; tolerable upper intake level 40 mg/day of elemental zinc. Doses are expressed as elemental zinc, which differs from the zinc sulfate salt weight. Refer to current product labeling.
medicines.storage: Store below 30 C, protected from light and moisture (WHO-prequalified dispersible tablets); follow the label of the specific product.
